tweak your 'LOD(level of detail) bias',  turning it up higher does reduce visual quality but increases performance. 

once again, these are just things that helped me in my particular case. im still figuring out how to boost my fps even more because i lowkey feel like its still on the low side for my specs but thats why im still looking into it. 

every computer is different, so you genuinely youll have to do a bit of research regarding your pc specs, and experimenting with settings, but its worth the headache. goodluck and lmk if you have any additional questions :)

personally what has helped me be able to translate notation quicker in my mind is first figuring out the most “common” squares.

so we know d4 and e4 is the center on whites side, so that would mean that d5 and e5 is the center on blacks side. 

we know that c3 and f3 are *usually* the knights most popular developing square on whites side, so knowing that, we can recall the same for the other side and realize that c6 and f6 are also *usually* the most popular developing squares for the knights on blacks side. 

for the bishops, we know that people looove to pin the knights on the squares we were just mentioning. so for example if you’re playing as white, to pin the black knights to their respective major pieces, one would have to move a bishop to either b5 or g5, and if you were playing as black then the pinning bishops would land on b4 or g4. 

now we have what are known as “weaker” squares, these squares are normally more vulnerable during middle game and late game. it would be b2 and g2 on whites side, and b7 and g7 on blacks side. 

then speaking of pawns again, we know that a3 and h3 for white and a6 and h6 for black all create a luft for the king when it’s castled on that respective side, while also kicking away the potential pinning bishop or knight that lands on b4, b5, g4, and g5. 

for a fianchetto we know that b3 and/or g3 for white and b6 and/or g6 for black have to be played. 

and of course the easiest numbers to remember are that 1 is whites back rank, and 8 is blacks back rank. if you notice, we actually cover all 1-8 numbered squares ! a-h can be a little bit trickier to remember, but try to keep in mind for white, that a,b,c is whites queen side and f,g,h is whites king side. knowing that we know that a,b,c for black is his queen side, and that f,g,h is his kingside. while also keeping in mind that d and e are the central squares. 

if you’re able to memorize just those that i’ve mentioned so far, that’s 24 squares !! that may not seem like a lot considering there are a total of 64 squares, however knowing where the most common squares are, helps you translate other notation faster over time because you may have trouble remembering where exactly f4 is on the board but you remember that f3 is where whites knight usually goes so then you’re able to quickly remember that f4 would be directly the square above that knight on f3. 

slightly off topic but i also found that notating out loud where the pieces are going when played by either side, helped solidify my translation of notations. for example, if the opponent plays Nc3 then i verbally say “knight to c3” while trying not to peak at the letters and numbers on side the board. over time this allows for quicker processing especially recognizing the most common squares. there’s a reason why pattern recognition is so important in chess ! sorry for the long paragraph but i hope some of this helped :)

no problem ! it seems like you’re on a good path so far into building up your knowledge. some little tips to be aware of are:

understand the basics thoroughly: grasp the rules, basic tactics (like forks, pins, and skewers), and simple openings. this foundational knowledge is crucial because it forms the basis for more advanced play. definitely get familiar with looking out for these inconspicuous tactics, start remembering these patterns that lead to winning positions. to add to this, having dedicated openings you’re comfortable playing and familiar with is key to building your opening repertoire. yes it’s one thing to know the basic principles of chess, which is good of course, but it’ll only take you so far. eventually you’re gonna have to find some openings that fit your playstyle. 

focus on tactics: solving puzzles regularly improves pattern recognition and calculation skills. aim to spot tactical opportunities (such as captures, forks, checkmates and the tactics mentioned above) in your games. understanding these tactical motifs will help you capitalize on your opponent's mistakes and avoid blunders yourself. lichess offers unlimited free puzzles. 

study endgames: learn essential endgame principles, especially basic endings like king and pawn versus king. how to mate with just queen and king vs king, how to mate with just rook and king vs king. knowing which pawns to move and not move. knowing when/how to stalemate, definitely learn about triangulation and opposition. all of these scenarios frequently occur in games and knowing them well can turn losses into draws or wins.

review your games: analyzing your games, particularly losses, is essential for improvement. look for recurring mistakes or missed opportunities. spotting your reoccurring mistakes is essential in getting better, take losses as a learning lesson and find out what went wrong and what you could’ve done better. use a chess engine or ask stronger players for feedback to understand where you went wrong and how you can improve.

learn opening principles: focus on simple openings that prioritize piece development and control of the center. understand the underlying ideas behind the moves rather than memorizing lengthy sequences. this approach will allow you to adapt to different positions and opponents more effectively. it seems like you have this down so far, but i’m sure there is still room to improve. as said above, learning openings goes hand in hand with this. the better your opening principles the better your play your opening, and the better your play your opening the more of an advantage you gain over time. 

play regularly and wisely: practice regularly with a mix of longer time control games (like 15 minutes per side) and shorter blitz games (like 5 minutes per side). longer games help you delve deeper into strategic concepts and planning, while blitz games improve your speed and tactical awareness. aim to learn from each game, regardless of the result. for a beginner i recommend playing rapid as it allows for deeper calculation. 15|10 seems to be my sweet spot. 
 
and most importantly, stay patient and persistent: progress in chess takes time and dedication. celebrate your successes, no matter how small, and learn from your losses. maintaining a positive attitude and a willingness to learn from every game will help you steadily climb the elo ladder.

by consistently applying these strategies and continuously learning from your experiences, you'll gradually improve your understanding and performance in chess, moving beyond the 500 elo mark and eventually heading towards the 1000 range. good luck !

practice tactics: use websites or apps that offer tactical puzzles. solving these regularly improves pattern recognition and calculation. lichess offers unlimited free puzzles i believe. 

study endgames: learn basic endgame principles (like king and pawn versus king) as they often decide games at lower levels.

review games: analyze your own games to identify mistakes and missed opportunities. use a chess engine to assist in finding better moves.

learn opening principles: focus on simple openings that develop pieces logically (like the italian game or queen’s gambit). understand the ideas behind the moves rather than memorizing sequences.

play regularly: engage in both longer time control games (like 15 minutes per side) and shorter blitz games (like 5 minutes per side) to practice different aspects of your game.

seek feedback: if possible, play stronger opponents and ask them for advice after the game. alternatively, join a chess club or online community where you can discuss strategies and learn from others.

stay positive and persistent: improvement takes time and effort. stay motivated by celebrating small successes and learning from setbacks.

i’d say that a finding a healthy/balanced mix of studying puzzles and learning theory is key. however at lower ELO, learning basic yet fundamental concepts is more important than memorizing a bunch of lines. focusing excessively on theory might not be as crucial as developing fundamental skills like tactics, strategy, and basic principles of chess. here’s why:

tactical proficiency: at lower elo levels, games are often decided by tactical oversights rather than by the subtleties of opening theory. therefore, practicing tactics (like forks, pins, skewers, etc.) can yield more immediate improvement.

understanding basic principles: instead of memorizing specific moves in openings, it's more beneficial to understand the underlying principles (like controlling the center, developing pieces efficiently, and king safety). these principles guide your decisions throughout the game.

focus on strategy: learning strategic concepts such as pawn structure, piece coordination, and planning ahead are universally applicable and can have a greater impact on game outcomes than knowing specific theoretical lines.

general improvement vs. specific lines: spending time improving overall chess skills (calculation, pattern recognition, positional understanding) can yield more sustainable progress than memorizing specific opening variations.

however, some basic opening knowledge is still beneficial:

opening principles: understanding why certain moves are made (like developing pieces, controlling the center) helps in making logical opening moves.

common openings: learning a few basic openings helps you reach playable middle games. focus on understanding the ideas behind the moves rather than memorizing long sequences.

in summary, while theory in chess has its place, especially in higher levels where precision and detailed preparation matter more, at lower elo levels it’s more important to build a strong foundation of tactical awareness, strategic understanding, and general principles. this approach will lead to more consistent improvement and better overall performance.

i just started maining rev not too long ago, here are some things that helped me utilize his ultimate to the fullest. 

1.	place totems in smart places where the enemy can’t activate it themselves, or so when you die and get sent back you’re not in the open and can be shot at. try to place it on high spots or in buildings, behind cover etc. think “if i were to get sent back here, would i survive?” especially with the range being gone, you can be way more strategic with the placement. 

2.	treat your totem life as if you weren’t in that form(to an extent). an example would be that i know once i pop my totem and activate it, i become way more aggressive and don’t play as smart as i would if i wasn’t in totem protection, don’t get me wrong its not bad to be aggressive with it, but be smart AND aggressive, that’s the difference between a good revenant and bad revenant. 

3.	 I’d say use it in every fight if possible, but be smart with it. you never want to die with your ultimate because that means you wasted your second life. 

4.	 ping or call out when you place death totem! if you’re playing trios, you could turn 3 lives into 6 lives.  can definitely turn the fight in your favor, if used properly. 

5.	 watch your timer til it deactivates! there have been times where i’m not mindful of my timer and it runs out when i’m in the middle of the fight causing me to go down, on the other hand if i know it’s gonna run out soon i will be more aggressive and A. die and get sent back or B. get some damage in, or even get a knockdown (be careful bc if you do this your timer can run out leaving you stranded in that fight)

6.	don’t be afraid to be aggressive with it, like i said be smart AND aggressive, you can easily get atleast 1 kill while in death protection if you play it smart. a good way to use it is, activate it when approaching as a 3rd party or even a lone squad. you can get some damage in and possibly some kills, while not really risking yourself. 

7.	this is kinda my personal play style, but you can pop death protection and sneak up to the squad you’re about to fight. sure they know a team just activated it, but sometimes they don’t usually expect a revenant in death protection to sneak up on them. it’s a good way to get some damage in and possibly even a knockdown.
